messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Malik was seven years old when he watched his mother pressed against a wall in their living room, his father’s hand clamped over her mouth. It lasted maybe two minutes, but what he carried forward were snapshots—frozen frames: the lamp knocked sideways, the sound of her breathing, the way his own body had gone rigid on the stairs, one hand gripping the banister. He could still feel that posture when the memories came, as if his muscles remembered before his mind did. He had not spoken of it since. He had never told anyone that what he remembered most was the silence that followed—the long, thick quiet after his father walked out—and how in that silence he had understood, even at seven, that nothing he could do would ever stop bad things from happening.

Now eighteen, Malik had become a police officer. He told himself it was a way to be the person who showed up when others couldn’t. But the job had not given him control. It had given him a city full of unfamiliar streets, and every time he entered a new building or walked a strange corridor, he scanned for something he could not name. He noticed potential weapons everywhere—a crowbar in a truck bed, the shape of a bottle in someone’s hand, the glint of a kitchen knife through an open window. This vigilance, he believed, was the only thing keeping him safe. He had come to trust his own judgment less and less; he was certain that if he let his guard down, he would miss something, and then something terrible would happen, and it would be his fault. He could not rely on himself, so he relied on suspicion.

Unusual silence was the worst. On patrol, when a block went quiet—no voices, no traffic—his chest would tighten and his mind would deliver a single image: his mother’s face, frozen in that snapshot, her eyes wide. The memory would land in his body before he could stop it. He would feel his seven-year-old posture return, his hand reaching for his holster the way it had once gripped the banister. And then the silence itself would feel dangerous, as though it were waiting. He had begun to avoid unfamiliar places entirely, sticking to routes he knew, refusing backup assignments that took him outside his precinct. He told his sergeant he preferred solo patrol. What he did not say was that being alone meant he could control the environment—no unexpected touches, no one stepping into his space without warning. Being touched unprepared made him flinch, and the flinch embarrassed him, and the embarrassment fed a growing fear that his reactions meant he was going crazy.

The grief came without warning. A domestic call in a quiet apartment building—a woman with a bruised cheek, a man standing in the kitchen—and Malik’s mind snapped to his mother’s face again, and he felt a wave of sorrow that had nowhere to go. He could not process it in the moment. He could only stand there, his body in that old frozen position, and then afterward, alone in his patrol car, he would tell himself that he was broken, that his own instincts could not be trusted, that he would never be the officer he needed to be. These thoughts made him more watchful. He began to interpret ordinary behavior as suspicious: a man checking his phone too quickly, a teenager standing too still, a woman walking too fast. Every ambiguous cue felt like a threat. And every threat, once noticed, triggered another memory—another snapshot of that night—and the loop tightened.

He had stopped going out with friends months ago. He did not visit his mother. He worked double shifts because the station felt predictable. But even there, the silence in the locker room after everyone left made him pull his gun mid-check, hands shaking. That was the moment he finally called the department’s mental health line. He was terrified that he was losing his grip, but what he said aloud was quieter: he was tired of being afraid of silence.
